To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

corticospinal excitability is suppressed before a response is selected in a choice reaction time paradigm and that this suppression persists after the imperative has been presented when the selected response is a homologous effector.

the suppression of corticospinal excitability during response selection can be dissociated into two distinct processes: (i) a process that is engaged during response selection and is specific to the response selected and (ii) a process that occurs in advance of the imperative signal and is independent of the response that is eventually selected.
corticospinal excitability in the selected hand is reduced during response selection, and that this reduction is not due to a general increase in inhibitory tone during high anticipation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying response selection and the preparation of action.
the neural mechanisms of motor response selection, and the role of inhibitory processes in this context.
the role of inhibition in motor preparation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the inhibition is not related to the anticipation, but rather to the response selection.
the inhibition of motor output in response preparation is a result of both anticipatory and selection processes.

the corticospinal system is inhibited before the imperative stimulus, regardless of response selection and the degree of anticipation, and that this inhibition is released when the selected response occurs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inhibition of corticospinal excitability during response selection occurs in a competitive fashion and is modulated by response selection processes.
the corticospinal system is engaged by both the selection of an action, and by the anticipation of an upcoming event.
the inhibitory processes engaged in response selection are dissociable from those engaged in anticipation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inhibition of motor output is not a unitary phenomenon.
inhibition of the selected response can occur in the absence of any advance preparation, suggesting that inhibition is an important part of the response selection process.
the inhibition of motor responses is not only related to processes associated to response preparation but also to processes related to the competition between potential responses.
